Magnesium: low and high, mild / moderate / severe

Hospitalist Toolkit · Electrolytes tab · adults · SI units · normal Mg 0.70–1.00 mmol/L (1.7–2.4 mg/dL) · magnesium sulfate 2 g (8 mmol) or 5 g (20 mmol)
Decision-support draft, not verified. Written by Claude; doses are typical adult doses. Check against Island Health protocols and pharmacy. Guideline = stated in a guideline; Practice = common practice (no guideline sets this).

Low magnesium (hypomagnesemia)

MildModerateSevere
Mg (mmol/L)0.60–0.690.50–0.59< 0.50, or tetany, seizure, arrhythmia
Symptoms / ECGOften none; low K or Ca that will not correctTremor, cramps, weakness; long QTTetany, Chvostek / Trousseau, seizures, confusion; AF, VT, torsades; digoxin toxicity
TreatmentPO target 20 mmol/day: Mg 250 mg elemental tab BID, or Mg Rougier 30 mL TID Local sheet. MgSO4 2 g / 50 mL IV if low K/Ca, arrhythmia or long QTMg < 0.6: MgSO4 5 g in 100 mL NS IV, max 2 g/h Local sheetTorsades / seizure: MgSO4 2 g IV over 10–15 min (crash-cart vials). Then MgSO4 5 g IV, max 2 g/h (slower keeps more); often a second dose
GFR < 30 / dialysis50% dose Local sheetMgSO4 2 g, recheck before moreMgSO4 2 g at a time, recheck before more
Repeat labs Local sheetNext morning, then daily while replacingAt least 1 h after IV; 72 h level more accurateAt least 1 h after IV, then daily; cardiac monitor until QT shortens

Causes of low Mg

  • GI: diarrhea, laxatives, high-output stoma, malabsorption, pancreatitis, long-term PPI, alcohol, malnutrition
  • Kidney: loop/thiazide diuretics, alcohol, glycosuria / DKA, aminoglycosides, amphotericin, cisplatin, tacrolimus/cyclosporine, foscarnet, pentamidine, cetuximab/panitumumab, Gitelman
  • Shift: refeeding, insulin, hungry bone after parathyroidectomy
  • Unclear cause: fractional excretion of Mg > 2–4% = kidney loss; < 2% = GI or intake

Good to know

  • Serum Mg is < 1% of body Mg: a normal level does not rule out depletion
  • Much of IV Mg is lost in the urine: slower rates keep more (max 2 g/h) Local sheet
  • 2 g = 8 mmol; 24 mg elemental Mg = 1 mmol Local sheet
  • Replace Mg first or with K and Ca: they will not correct otherwise
  • Stop or reduce a PPI if no firm indication; amiloride or spironolactone for diuretic loss

High magnesium (hypermagnesemia)

MildModerateSevere
Mg (mmol/L)1.01–1.992.0–2.99≥ 3.0, or symptoms (lost reflexes, hypotension, drowsiness, slow breathing)
Symptoms / ECGNoneNausea, flushing, headache, drowsiness, reduced reflexes3–5: lost patellar reflexes, hypotension, bradycardia, long PR/QRS, ileus. > 5: respiratory paralysis, complete heart block, arrest
TreatmentStop magnesium intake; falls on its own if kidneys workStop all Mg; IV saline + furosemide 20–40 mg IV if kidneys work and volume allowsStop all Mg; calcium gluconate 10% 10–20 mL (1–2 g) IV over 10 min (repeat as needed); cardiac monitor; support breathing; dialysis if eGFR low or Mg stays ≥ 3 with symptoms
Repeat labs PracticeNext routine bloodsEvery 12–24 h; reflexes each shiftMg, Ca, K, creatinine every 4–6 h until < 2.0; patellar reflexes, respiratory rate, BP hourly

Causes of high Mg

  • Load + low eGFR (most cases): milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide), magnesium citrate / Pico-Salax / Citro-Mag bowel prep, Mg antacids and enemas, supplements, IV magnesium sulfate
  • Low excretion: AKI, CKD, lithium, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency
  • Shift out: tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, DKA before insulin

Good to know

  • Loss of patellar reflexes comes before respiratory depression: check reflexes
  • Calcium only buys time; dialysis removes Mg
  • Avoid Mg-containing laxatives with eGFR < 30

Sources

Local electrolyte replacement sheet (Richard Wanbon, PharmD, Dec 22, 2014): products, doses, rates and timing of levels marked Local sheet. It is from 2014: confirm with pharmacy. The grading of severity and the high-magnesium section are common practice (no single guideline).
